title: Deepfakes & AI-Powered Scams
summary: Cloned voices, fake video calls and AI-written lures, and the habits that beat them.

lessons.title: Seeing is no longer believing
points: Deepfakes are AI-generated or altered video, images or audio that imitate real people.
Voice cloning can produce a convincing copy of someone's voice from a short sample of their speech.
AI also writes flawless phishing messages in any language, so spelling mistakes are no longer a reliable clue.

lessons.title: A real case
points: In early 2024, a finance employee in engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office joined a video call with what looked and sounded like the CFO and colleagues.
All of them were deepfakes. The employee made 15 transfers totalling HK$200 million (about US$25 million).
He had initially suspected the request was phishing. The realistic video call is what convinced him.

lessons.title: Verify the request, not the face
points: For money, credentials or sensitive data, confirm through a separate, known channel: call back on a number you already have.
Agree a family or team 'safe word' or verification question for urgent requests.
Organisations should require two people to approve large or unusual payments.
lessons.tip: Urgency + secrecy + money = stop and verify, no matter how real it looks.

lessons.title: Clues and limits
points: Possible signs: odd lip-sync, unnatural blinking or lighting, robotic tone, refusing to switch channels or answer personal questions.
Detection tools and visual clues aren't reliable on their own. Good deepfakes can show none of these signs.
Process beats perception: verification steps work even when you can't tell it's fake.

questions.q: Your 'manager' calls with a slightly odd but familiar voice asking for an urgent supplier payment. What's the best action?
options: Hang up and call them back on their known number or verify via a separate channel
Ask them to email instead and then pay
Ask a colleague to pay instead
questions.why: Voices can be cloned. Out-of-band verification through a channel you already trust defeats voice and video impersonation.

questions.q: If you can see someone on a live video call, you can be sure it's really them.
questions.why: Real-time deepfake video exists. In the Arup case, every other participant on the call was fake.

questions.q: In the 2024 Arup deepfake case, roughly how much money was transferred?
questions.why: The employee made 15 transfers totalling HK$200 million, about US$25 million, after a deepfake video call.

questions.q: Which control best protects an organisation from deepfake payment fraud?
options: Two-person approval and call-back verification for payments
questions.why: Process controls work regardless of how convincing the fake is.

questions.q: Because AI writes fluent text, perfect grammar no longer means a message is safe.
questions.why: Attackers use AI to write polished lures. Focus on the request, the sender and the channel.

questions.q: What is a 'safe word' used for?
options: A pre-agreed phrase to verify a caller's identity in urgent situations
A way to unlock your phone
questions.why: A secret phrase agreed in person is hard for a scammer to know, even with a cloned voice.

questions.q: Deepfake detection tools are 100% reliable, so you can skip verification if a tool says a call is genuine.
questions.why: Detection is imperfect. Keep verification processes in place for sensitive requests.

questions.q: A video of a public figure endorsing an investment app goes viral. What's the safest reaction?
options: Invest quickly before it sells out
Be sceptical, as celebrity deepfake endorsements are a common scam
Click the link to learn more
questions.why: Deepfaked endorsements are widely used in investment scams. Check the person's official channels and regulated sources.

sources.title: CNN – Arup revealed as victim of US$25 million deepfake scam (May 2024)
FBI IC3 PSA – Criminals use generative AI to facilitate financial fraud (Dec 2024)
